summary: Describes version two of Microsoft's PPP CHAP dialect, which is similar to but incompatible with version one. It documents a vendor challenge-based authentication method. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: MS-CHAP-V2 lets a caller prove knowledge of a password without sending the password itself. The server also sends a value that the caller checks, so both sides can authenticate each other.

subtitle: A PPP challenge-response method that asks each side to verify the other.

tldr.problem: The first Microsoft version of PPP CHAP did not authenticate the server to the peer. Its successor also changes some packet fields, so it is not compatible with version one.
tldr.mechanism: MS-CHAP-V2 uses a challenge from the authenticator and a peer-generated challenge in the response. The success message carries a value the peer checks to authenticate the server.
tldr.outcome: The memo defines packet formats, password-change behavior and calculation procedures for this Microsoft CHAP dialect. It is Informational, not an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2759 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Version Two Adds
sections.content:
RFC 2759 describes Microsoft's version two dialect of the Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP) for the Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP). It is similar to MS-CHAP-V1 but incompatible with it because some fields are removed or assigned different meanings.

PPP negotiates this dialect using CHAP Algorithm value 0x81 in the Link Control Protocol (LCP). The main addition is mutual authentication: the peer sends a challenge in its response, and the authenticator returns a value the peer must verify.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller answers a challenge, and the server must answer a check of its own. This lets each side check that the other knows the shared password.

sections.title: Challenge and Response Fields
sections.content:
The authenticator's Challenge packet contains a 16-octet value. The peer's Response packet carries a 16-octet Peer-Challenge, 8 reserved octets set to zero, a 24-octet NT-Response and a Flags octet set to zero.

The NT-Response is calculated from the password, user name, peer challenge and authenticator challenge. The calculation uses the account name without any domain prefix. The password itself is not sent in the Response packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller sends two random challenge values and a calculated answer, not the password. The server and caller use the same defined calculation to check that answer.

sections.title: Success, Failure and Password Change
sections.content:
A Success message contains S= followed by 40 hexadecimal digits. The peer MUST verify this authenticator response; if the value is missing or incorrect, it MUST end the session. A Failure message includes an error code, whether a retry is allowed, a new challenge and a password-change version.

The Change-Password packet is used when the authenticator reports that the password expired. It has Code 7 and Length 586. The packet carries encrypted password material and a response calculated using the new password.
sections.plainLanguage: A successful login is not complete until the caller checks the server's response. If the password expired, a separate packet can carry a protected password change.

sections.title: How the Authentication Values Are Made
sections.content:
The RFC gives pseudocode for deriving the response fields. The challenge hash uses SHA-1 with the two challenges and the user name; the password hash uses MD4. The challenge response uses DES operations on pieces of the password hash.

The authenticator response is derived from the password hash, NT-Response and challenge data, then encoded as a text string. The RFC also specifies encryption steps for the password-change fields and supplies worked examples.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC fixes a recipe for turning the password and challenges into values both sides can check. It also defines the calculations needed to protect a password change.

sections.title: Limiting Password Guessing
sections.content: The security section recommends that an authenticator limit the number of password retries. This makes brute-force guessing more difficult. The examples include a case where authentication stops allowing retries after repeated failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The server should limit retries so an attacker cannot keep testing password guesses without end.
